topline: Four stories today: Abu Dhabi talks yield a prisoner-swap deal but no ceasefire while Europe waits outside the room, about 50 leaders gather in Dublin for the European Political Community with Ukraine and the UK–EU reset in focus, Brussels unveils a Digital Fairness Act against dark patterns and subscription traps, and NATO jets miss a drone over Lithuania after a night of Baltic air alerts.

stories.title: Abu Dhabi talks end with a prisoner-swap deal but no ceasefire, and Europe kept outside the room
stories.summary: Two days of US-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi ended on 11 November with agreement in principle on a large exchange of prisoners of war, but no progress on a ceasefire or territory. Ukraine's team was led by Rustem Umerov, Russia's by Vladimir Medinsky, with US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff mediating. Zelensky said around 1,000 prisoners per side had been discussed, possibly rising to 1,500; final numbers were due to be set on 12 November. Kushner said there is currently no trust between the sides and that European partners should be at the table, an idea he and Witkoff plan to raise with Putin in Moscow before flying to Dublin to brief Zelensky. EU, German, French, British, Italian and NATO officials were in Abu Dhabi but met only the US and Ukrainian teams, as Russia refused to see them.
stories.why: The EU is Ukraine's largest financial backer yet has no seat in the negotiations that could redraw Europe's security order, an imbalance leaders will confront in Dublin this week.

left.angle: Left-leaning coverage presents the swap as a limited humanitarian result of talks that otherwise stalled, and gives prominence to the dispute over Europe's role, setting Russian dismissal of the Europeans against Kyiv's insistence that European security cannot be settled without Europe. It spends less time on the mechanics of the US mediation.

outlets.name: Al Jazeera
outlets.note: Swap as the only concrete outcome; foregrounds Medinsky's dismissal of the EU against Zelensky's calls for European involvement.

outlets.name: CNN
outlets.note: Headline leads with Trump's envoys heading to Moscow after talks ended without a breakthrough.

right.angle: Right-leaning coverage leads with Europe and Britain being shut out, treating the exclusion as a measure of the continent's weak leverage; the Telegraph turns it into a UK story about London seeking its own channel to the Kremlin. Both stress that territory remains the core obstacle and that results so far are humanitarian rather than political.

outlets.name: The Telegraph
outlets.note: Syndicated piece on Britain being sidelined and Moscow saying it would take a call from London's defence secretary.

outlets.name: Brussels Signal
outlets.note: Portrays EU involvement as reactive and uncertain, with Russian officials telling Europeans to wait at their hotel.

stories.differ: Left-leaning outlets frame Europe's absence as a diplomatic wrong Kyiv is resisting; right-leaning outlets frame it as evidence of European, and British, weakness that needs a harder-headed fix.

stories.title: Around 50 European leaders meet in Dublin as Ukraine and the UK–EU reset dominate the agenda
stories.summary: The ninth European Political Community summit opens in Dublin on 12 November, co-chaired by Taoiseach Micheál Martin and European Council President António Costa, with around 50 leaders including Zelensky, Macron, Merz, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham and NATO's Mark Rutte. The informal format produces no binding decisions; sessions cover hybrid threats, economic and democratic resilience, Moldova and Armenia, and a roundtable on European security, where Macron is expected to present principles for the continent's future security. Ukraine faces an estimated €70bn gap in its 2027 budget. Burnham, arriving from COP31, is expected to announce further Russia sanctions and is looking ahead to a UK–EU summit on 20 November where agrifood, emissions-trading and youth-mobility deals are under negotiation. EU-27 leaders meet informally on 13 November on artificial intelligence, with a Ukraine debate and an EU peace envoy also on the table.
stories.why: Dublin is the EU's main chance this week to show unity on Ukraine while it is outside the US-led talks, and a staging post for the largest UK–EU rapprochement since Brexit.

left.angle: We found no left-leaning piece on the summit itself from 10–12 November. Earlier coverage from EUobserver, published 9 November, framed Dublin around Ukraine as the real agenda behind the official AI theme, and as a test of EU unity while Europe is excluded from the US-brokered talks; it did not dwell on the UK reset.

outlets.name: EUobserver (earlier coverage, 9 Nov)
outlets.note: Week-ahead piece: Russia's war is the unspoken centre of the Dublin meetings; Costa added a Ukraine debate.

right.angle: Right-leaning British coverage treats the gathering mainly through the Brexit lens, warning that Burnham's reset slides towards rejoining the EU and highlighting David Cameron's caution against that. Ukraine and the security agenda get little attention in these pieces.

outlets.name: Daily Mail (front page, via PA papers round-up)
outlets.note: Front page leads on Cameron telling the PM not to rejoin, casting Dublin as a sales pitch for a 'Brexit betrayal'.

outlets.name: The Spectator Australia (earlier opinion, 9 Nov)
outlets.note: Argues the reset concedes on food standards, energy payments and mobility for a small economic gain.

stories.differ: Pro-EU coverage sees Dublin as a Ukraine-and-unity summit; right-leaning UK outlets see it as a stage for a Brexit rollback they oppose.

stories.title: Commission proposes Digital Fairness Act to curb dark patterns, subscription traps and loot boxes for minors
stories.summary: Consumer commissioner Michael McGrath presented the Digital Fairness Act on 11 November, a regulation that would replace the 2005 Unfair Commercial Practices Directive. It bans manipulative interface design outright for a list of practices such as fake scarcity claims, requires free trials to need active consent before turning into paid plans, and makes online cancellation easy, with a right to reach a human. Users would be able to switch off addictive features like infinite scroll and autoplay, paid loot boxes would be banned for under-18s, and influencer ads would need clear disclosure with brands sharing liability. Fines could reach 6% of global turnover, and the Commission estimates €13.7bn a year in consumer benefits against €678m in business costs. Industry group CCIA said the text overlaps with existing EU law, and German press publishers warned it threatens their subscription models.
stories.why: It is the EU's next big piece of platform regulation, landing as Brussels promises to cut red tape and as US pressure on EU tech rules continues; Parliament and Council negotiations are expected to take years.

left.angle: Left-leaning and pro-regulation coverage leads with the crackdown on manipulative design and influencer marketing, and relays consumer and digital-rights groups who welcome it but say it does not go far enough, notably because addictive features are opt-out rather than banned. Industry objections receive brief treatment.

outlets.name: EUobserver
outlets.note: Based on the leaked draft; quotes BEUC and EDRi, who warn opt-outs leave 'significant uncertainty'.

right.angle: The centre-right coverage we found leads with business alarm rather than consumer gains, foregrounding German press publishers who say the rules endanger digital subscription and advertising models. We found no other right-leaning outlet covering the proposal in this window.

outlets.name: FAZ
outlets.note: Publishers' associations say they are dismayed by the new EU digital law.

stories.differ: One side asks whether the act protects consumers enough; the other asks whether it damages the businesses, including newspapers, that depend on subscriptions and ads.

stories.title: NATO jets twice fail to down a drone over Lithuania during a night of Baltic air alerts
stories.summary: Lithuania issued air alerts across several regions on the night of 10–11 November, briefly raising them to red, and closed Vilnius and Kaunas airports, affecting around 400 passengers. Officials said four drones were detected in Belarus and one crossed into Lithuania near Druskininkai, then flew north through Latvia and Estonia into Russia. NATO jets made two unsuccessful attempts to shoot it down, with missile debris later found near Biržai; officials have not said which country's aircraft fired. The military said the drone's type and origin are unconfirmed and suggested it may have been diverted by electronic warfare during Ukraine's drone strikes on Russia that night. President Gitanas Nausėda warned such incursions may happen again, and the prime minister promised a full investigation.
stories.why: Repeated incursions test NATO and EU air defences on the eastern flank and feed the debate over drone defences and the cost of protecting EU airspace.

left.angle: Left-leaning coverage we found treats the Baltic alerts as one strand of an escalating exchange of strikes between Russia and Ukraine, stressing that the drones' origin is unclear and leaving out the missed interceptions and airport closures. We found no major European left-leaning title covering the incident in detail.

outlets.name: Al Jazeera
outlets.note: Wire-based roundup; the Baltic alerts appear as a side note to Russia–Ukraine strikes.

right.angle: Right-leaning Italian outlets lead with NATO's failure to hit the target, the threat coming from Belarus and the disruption to flights and residents, while noting the drone's origin is not confirmed. Il Giornale's live blog places it inside wider war coverage that also relays Russian official claims.

outlets.name: Secolo d'Italia
outlets.note: Headline built on NATO jets firing twice and missing; stresses closed airports.

outlets.name: Il Giornale
outlets.note: Live blog on drone alerts over Europe and NATO scrambles, with the object entering from Belarus.

stories.differ: Right-leaning coverage makes NATO's miss and the Belarus border the story; left-leaning coverage folds the alerts into the wider Russia–Ukraine war and stresses uncertainty over origin.

right.title: European Commission drops bid to make 'hate speech' an EU crime
